## The lodge
Name: Sample Bush Lodge.
Host: Naledi. Guests reach the host fastest on WhatsApp. Messages to the host are written in English.
Address: Sample Bush Lodge, 1 Sample Road, Sampletown, Limpopo.
Time zone: Africa/Johannesburg.

## Rooms and what is included
- River Suite (sleeps 2): King bedroom, bathroom with outdoor shower, private deck over the riverbed with plunge pool, air conditioning and fans.
- Marula Suite (sleeps 2): King bedroom, bathroom with bath and outdoor shower, shaded deck with day bed, air conditioning and fans.
- Baobab Suite (sleeps 2 to 3): King or twin beds, a day bed for a child, outdoor shower, private deck with braai.
- Family Villa (sleeps 4 to 6): Two bedrooms with their own bathrooms, lounge, kitchen, shaded deck with braai and a private pool.

## Getting to the lodge
- Fly to Hoedspruit: The easy way in. About 25 to 30 minutes from the airport to your lodge. Allow about 30 minutes of driving, plus 30 minutes at the airport for bags and car hire.
  - Airlink flies to Hoedspruit Eastgate from Johannesburg (just under an hour) and Cape Town. Check the current timetable, because routes change.
  - Car hire is available at the airport. Book ahead in school holidays.
  - Send your host your flight number so they know when to expect you.
- Fly to Nelspruit and drive: Kruger Mpumalanga International, then about 2 hours 45 minutes by road (147 km), via the R538 and R40. Allow about 165 minutes of driving, plus 40 minutes at the airport for bags and car hire.
  - Hire a car at the airport and set off in good time, so you arrive in daylight.
  - Fill the tank and stock up in Hoedspruit town, 7 km from the lodge.
- Drive from Johannesburg: About 435 km and 6 hours without stops. Plan for 7 hours, and start early. Allow about 360 minutes of driving, plus 45 minutes at the airport for bags and car hire.
  - Leave early so you arrive before sunset. Avoid driving after dark: animals, pedestrians and poor lighting are the risks.
  - Most visitors save the drive and fly on to Hoedspruit instead (about an hour).
Guests should aim to arrive before sunset. Driving after dark is risky because of animals on the road.

- God's Window (130 min by road, 119 km). The classic Lowveld viewpoint, best early in the day.

## Good to know before travelling
- Passport and entry: Entry rules depend on your passport, so check your own government's travel advice. In general South Africa asks for a passport that stays valid for at least 30 days after you leave and has two blank pages, plus proof that you are leaving again. Children need their own travel document, and officials can ask for extra papers such as a birth certificate. Rules change, so check the official sources before you fly.
- Health and malaria: Hoedspruit lies in the Lowveld, a region where malaria occurs, mostly in the warm, wet months (roughly October to May). Talk to a doctor or travel clinic about preventive tablets, ideally a few weeks before you travel. Use insect repellent with DEET at dusk and at night and wear long sleeves in the evening. If you get a fever, see a doctor, even up to six months after your trip. Check your routine vaccinations; hepatitis A is commonly recommended.
- Insurance: Take travel insurance that covers medical care and repatriation. Private ambulance services can bill you directly, so keep your policy number handy.
- Driving: South Africans drive on the left. Limits are usually 120 km/h on highways, 100 km/h on open roads and 60 km/h in towns, and 50 km/h on tar and 40 km/h on gravel in Kruger Park. Avoid driving after dark: animals, pedestrians and poor lighting are the risks. Keep doors locked and windows up, leave nothing valuable on view, and do not pick up hitchhikers. Carry your licence. An international driving permit is often recommended, and car-hire firms may ask for one if your licence is not in English.
- Money and tipping: The currency is the South African rand (ZAR). Cards work in most shops and restaurants, and Hoedspruit has ATMs. Keep some cash for small purchases. A tip of 10 to 15 percent is usual in restaurants, and fuel attendants, who fill the tank for you, appreciate a few rand.
- Plugs and power: Power is 230 V at 50 Hz, the same as Europe, so your chargers work without a converter. The sockets are different: bring a Type M adapter, or a universal one that covers types M and N.
- Time zone: South Africa runs on SAST (UTC+2) all year, with no daylight saving. Sunrise is early in summer, around 05:00, so mornings start early.
- Phones and signal: Mobile reception can be poor in the bushveld, so WhatsApp and the lodge Wi-Fi are your friends. Download an offline map of the area before you arrive. Check roaming costs, or use a local SIM or eSIM.
- Staying safe: Use normal travel sense: lock the car and the lodge at night, and keep valuables out of sight. The estate's real hazards are wildlife and the road, so read the wildlife tips.

## Packing list
- Documents and money: Passports and a copy of each; Booking confirmation and flight tickets; Travel insurance details; Driving licence and international permit; Some rand in cash and a card that works abroad.
- Clothes: Light, loose clothes in neutral colours (green, khaki, brown); A warm layer for cool mornings and evenings; A light rain jacket for afternoon storms; Wide-brim hat and sunglasses; Closed shoes for walking outdoors; Swimwear.
- Wildlife: Binoculars; Camera with a zoom lens; Torch or headlamp for after dark; Refillable water bottle.
- Health: Insect repellent with DEET; Sunscreen (the UV index is often very high); Personal medicine, and malaria tablets if prescribed; Basic first-aid kit and hand sanitiser.
- Tech: Type M plug adapter; Power bank and phone charger; Offline maps downloaded.
- With children: Children's sun hats and swim shirts; Games and a wildlife spotting book for the car and patio; Children's own passports and any documents officials may ask for.

## Rules around wildlife
- Keep your distance and never walk towards an animal. Wild animals are not tame, however calm they look.
- Never feed wildlife. It makes animals bold and dangerous, and it is not allowed.
- No walking at night. After dark, use a torch, stay on lit paths and never go alone.
- Look before you step. Wear closed shoes outside at dusk, use a torch at night and shake out shoes left outdoors.
- Close doors and windows when you go out. Monkeys are expert kitchen thieves.
- Drive slowly and give animals right of way. They step onto roads at dusk, and a wait costs you nothing.
- If an animal blocks the road, wait quietly. Do not hoot, rev or edge forward.
- Do not leave food, rubbish or braai leftovers outside overnight.
- Keep noise down. The animals and your neighbours on the estate will thank you.

## Animals and birds
- Giraffe (on the estate, often seen; best time: morning and late afternoon). Very tall, with a long neck and brown patches. The tallest animal on earth. Adults reach about 5 metres and pull acacia leaves in with a tongue about 45 cm long. Calm, but they kick hard. Keep your distance and never walk towards one.
- Plains zebra (on the estate, often seen; best time: morning and afternoon, often at water). Black and white stripes. No two zebras match. Every zebra's stripe pattern is unique, like a fingerprint. Herds often graze alongside wildebeest and impala. Nervous and quick to bolt. Move slowly and keep your voice down.
- Blue wildebeest (on the estate, often seen; best time: morning and afternoon). Dark and shaggy, with a beard, a sloping back and curved horns. Bearded and shaggy, often seen with zebra. Calves can stand within minutes of birth and run within hours. Bulls can be touchy. Never approach on foot.
- Greater kudu (on the estate, often seen; best time: dawn and dusk). Grey-brown with thin white stripes and big round ears. Bulls have spiral horns. Bulls carry spiralling horns well over a metre long. Shy animals that can leap high fences. Kudu step onto roads at dusk. Drive slowly and watch the verges.
- Impala (on the estate, seen daily; best time: all day, most active early and late). Reddish-brown, with a black stripe on each side of the white rump. Males have lyre-shaped horns. The most common antelope in the Lowveld. Lambs arrive around the start of the rains, often from November. The first animals you'll meet. Don't startle herds on the road.
- Nyala (on the estate, often seen; best time: early morning and dusk, near thicket and water). Males are dark and shaggy with white stripes. Females are chestnut with thin stripes. A shy antelope of the thick bush near water. Males and females look so different that they can seem like two species. Look along the edge of the riverbed at first and last light.
- Waterbuck (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: morning and evening, at the riverbed). Shaggy grey-brown coat and a white ring on the rump. Males have long horns. It stays close to water, and the riverbed below the lodges is a good place to look. Males have long horns. Stay well back.
- Bushbuck (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: dusk and night). Chestnut with white spots and stripes. Shy and low to the ground. A shy antelope that hides in dense riverside bush and is active mostly at dusk and at night. Rarely seen in the open. Use a torch after dark.
- Common duiker (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: early and late). Small and grey-brown, with a tuft on the forehead. It darts into cover. 'Duiker' is Afrikaans for 'diver', because it dives into the bush when startled. Easy to miss. Look low, at the edge of the bush.
- Warthog (on the estate, often seen; best time: daytime). Grey and pig-like, with tusks and a tail held straight up when it runs. Sleeps in burrows and backs in, so the tusks face out. The tusks are sharp. Keep well away from sows with piglets.
- Vervet monkey (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: daytime). A small grey monkey with a black face and a long tail. Clever and cheeky. They learn to open doors and raid kitchens. Never feed them. Close doors and windows when you go out, and keep food and bins secure.
- Leopard (on the estate, rarely seen; best time: night and the hours around it). Golden coat with dark rosettes. Usually seen at night or resting in a tree. Reported on wildlife estates around Hoedspruit and seldom seen. Mostly active at night. Never walk alone after dark. If you see one, stay calm, do not run, keep your distance and tell your host. Sensitive species: never share where or when one was seen.
- African wild dog (on the estate, rarely seen; best time: early morning). Large round ears and a patchy coat of black, tan and white. Occasionally reported in the Hoedspruit area. Wild dogs hunt in packs and are endangered. A rare treat. Keep food and rubbish indoors overnight. Sensitive species: never share where or when one was seen.
- Spotted hyena (on the estate, rarely seen; best time: night and early morning). A sloping back, a spotted coat and round ears. Its whooping call carries far at night. Occasionally reported in the Hoedspruit area. Clans are led by females, and the whoop call is a way of keeping in touch. Keep food and rubbish indoors overnight and never leave bins outside.
- Bushbaby (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: after dark, from the patio). Tiny, with huge eyes and a fluffy tail. You will probably hear it before you see it. A small tree-dwelling primate whose cry sounds like a crying baby. Listen from the patio. Do not follow it into the dark.
- Honey badger (on the estate, rarely seen; best time: after dark, from the patio). Low and sturdy, dark below with a pale grey-white back. Famously fearless for its size, strong, clever and good at opening latches. Do not approach it. Secure bins and doors at night.
- Cape porcupine (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: after dark, from the patio). Low and round, with long black and white banded quills. Africa's largest rodent. It forages at night and its quills are modified hairs. Look, do not touch. Loose quills cause painful wounds.
- African civet (on the estate, sometimes seen; best time: after dark, from the patio). Dog-sized, with black and white markings and a dark mask. A solitary night forager that eats fruit, insects and small animals. Watch from the patio. Keep food and rubbish indoors.
- Lilac-breasted roller (on the estate, often seen; best time: early morning, on open branches). A lilac chest, a turquoise belly and long tail streamers. It dives from a perch to catch insects. The name comes from the rolling, tumbling display flights. Bring binoculars. It often sits on open branches near the road.
- Crested barbet (on the estate, seen daily; best time: early morning). Chunky, yellow and red-speckled, with a black crest. Its long, dry trill is one of the most common sounds of the bushveld. Listen first, then look in the tops of the tall trees.
- Burchell's starling (on the estate, seen daily; best time: daytime, often on the ground near the lodges). A large, glossy blue-green starling with a long tail and a pale eye. A bold, sociable bird that forages on the ground near the lodges. Please do not feed it. Wild birds are healthier on their own food.
- Yellow-billed hornbill (on the estate, often seen; best time: morning and afternoon). A long, curved yellow bill and a speckled back. Hornbills nest in tree holes, and the female is sealed in with mud while she raises the chicks. Common across the Lowveld bush. Look on the ground and in low branches.
- Grey go-away-bird (on the estate, often seen; best time: morning and afternoon). A slim grey bird with a pointed crest. Its harsh call sounds like "go away", which is how it got its name. Often the first to sound the alarm when a predator is near.
- African elephant (on day trips, often seen; best time: near water, mornings and afternoons). The largest land animal, grey, with a trunk and large ears. Herds are led by an experienced older female. In a park, stay in your vehicle with the engine off and give elephants space. Back away calmly if one flaps its ears or mock-charges.
- Lion (on day trips, sometimes seen; best time: dawn and dusk. they rest through the heat.). A tawny cat, and the males have a mane. Africa's most social big cat. Prides are built around related females. Never leave your vehicle in a park, and never get out to take a photo.
- African buffalo (on day trips, often seen; best time: morning and evening, near water). A heavy black bovine with a broad, curved horn boss. Herds can number in the hundreds. Unpredictable and dangerous. Stay in your vehicle.
- White rhino (on day trips, sometimes seen; best time: morning and afternoon). A huge grey animal with two horns and a wide, square lip. A grazer. Rhinos are targeted by poachers, so guides and parks never share exact locations. Please do not post where or when you saw one. Photos are fine, but switch off location tags. Sensitive species: never share where or when one was seen.
- Hippopotamus (on day trips, often seen; best time: in the water by day, on land at night). Round and grey, with eyes and nostrils above the water line. Spends the day in water and grazes on land at night. Dangerous. Stay well back from the water and never get between a hippo and the water.
- Nile crocodile (on day trips, often seen; best time: sunny mornings, on sandbanks). A long, armoured reptile that basks on sandbanks. Basks on sandbanks and slides into the water when disturbed. Never stand at the water edge, and never swim in rivers or dams.

## Extras guests can ask the host for
- Airport transfer: A lift between the airport and the lodge, arranged by your host. Price: the host confirms it.
- Braai pack: Food and firewood for a braai on your own patio. Your host tells you what is in the pack. Price: the host confirms it.
- Breakfast or dinner: A meal prepared for you, so a night off cooking. Tell your host about allergies and preferences. Price: the host confirms it.
- Open-vehicle game drive: A guided drive in an open safari vehicle. Your host suggests options and timing. Price: the host confirms it.
- Private bush dinner: Dinner by lantern light out in the bush, set up for your party only. Your host confirms the menu and the evening. Price: the host confirms it.
- Massage on your deck: A therapist comes to your suite. Your host confirms treatments, times and prices. Price: the host confirms it.
- Day trip to Kruger Park: Help planning a day in Kruger National Park, from the gate you use to what to bring. Price: the host confirms it.
- Panorama Route day: Advice for a full day at Blyde River Canyon, Bourke's Luck Potholes and God's Window. Price: the host confirms it.
Every extra is a request. Nothing is booked or charged in the app. The host confirms price and availability.
